tonic: The home chord or note, where the music feels at rest.
subdominant: Harmony that pulls away from home and sets up tension (the IV side).
dominant: The tension chord that wants to fall back to the tonic (the V).
borrowed: A chord taken from the parallel major/minor for extra color.
secondary dominant: A V chord aimed at a chord other than the tonic, briefly making it feel like home.
syncopation: Accents landing off the strongest beats, giving a pushed, lively feel.
voice leading: How each line moves note-to-note from one chord to the next.
parallel fifths: Two voices a 5th apart moving the same direction, the classic counterpoint no-no.
parallel octaves: Two voices an octave apart moving together, collapsing two lines into one.
hidden fifth: Both voices leap the same direction into a 5th, a softer parallel-5th.
hidden octave: Both voices leap the same direction into an octave.
contrary motion: Two voices moving in opposite directions. The most independent, strongest motion.
oblique motion: One voice holds while the other moves.
similar motion: Two voices moving the same direction by different amounts.
parallel motion: Two voices moving the same direction by the same interval.
density: How many notes sound at once or in quick succession. How full it feels.
register: How high or low the notes sit overall.
frequency: How many times per second something vibrates. In sound, faster means higher.
hertz: The unit for frequency: one hertz is one back-and-forth per second.
pitch: How high or low a note sounds, set by its frequency.
octave: The distance between a note and the note vibrating twice as fast. They sound like the same note, higher.
interval: The distance between two notes, counted in semitones and heard as a flavor.
beat: The steady pulse under music, the thing your foot taps.
bar: A group of beats, most often four, marked by the heavier grid lines.
tempo: How fast the beats come, measured in beats per minute (BPM).
meter: The repeating pattern that groups beats into bars: the count you keep without noticing.
downbeat: Beat one, the accented first beat of a bar, where the count starts over.
time signature: The two numbers, like 4/4, that say how many beats each bar holds and which grid division counts as one beat.
subdivision: The slicing of each beat into smaller equal parts: eighths, sixteenths, triplets.
triplet: Three equal slices where two would normally fit, giving a rolling, rounded feel.
grid: The piano roll's lattice of time slices; its width is the subdivision you are editing on.
quantize: Snapping notes to the grid, pulling every hit onto the nearest slice.
rest: A deliberate silence: a slice of counted time left empty on purpose.
tresillo: The 3+3+2 rhythm: two hits in a long stride, one arriving early, with the gap doing the pushing.
clave: The five-hit timekeeping pattern Afro-Cuban music is built around: a tresillo-shaped call, then a two-hit answer.
phrase: A run of notes heard as one musical sentence, with a shape and a breath at the end.
breath point: The gap where a line pauses to inhale before the next phrase begins.
call and response: One phrase asks and another answers: the question-and-answer pairing under most melodies.
leading tone: The note a semitone below home, which pulls strongly up to it.
mode: A scale defined by which of its notes is treated as home; the same notes yield a different mode from each starting point.
relative key: A major and minor key that share the exact same notes, differing only in which note is home (C major and A minor).
characteristic note: The one note that separates a mode from plain major or minor, the note that makes it that mode.
dorian: A minor mode brightened by a natural sixth: the hopeful minor of modal jazz and funk.
phrygian: A minor mode with a flat second: dark and tense, the Spanish and metal sound.
lydian: A major mode with a sharp fourth: floating and weightless, the wondrous major.
mixolydian: A major mode with a flat seventh: the bluesy, rock dominant that will not fully resolve.
locrian: The mode on the seventh degree, with a diminished home chord and no stable fifth, so it barely works as a key.
parallel key: A major and minor key sharing the same home note but different notes (C major and C minor): the pair borrowing pulls from.
modal interchange: Borrowing systematized: treating all seven parallel modes as one shared pantry of chords.
natural minor: Major with the 3rd, 6th, and 7th lowered a semitone: the default minor palette.
harmonic minor: Natural minor with the 7th raised back up, so the dominant chord pulls home again.
melodic minor: Natural minor with the 6th and 7th raised, so a line can climb to home in even steps.
parallel minor: The minor scale on the same home note: C major's parallel minor is C minor.
relative minor: The minor key sharing a major key's notes, home moved to its 6th degree: C major's relative is A minor.
semitone: The smallest step on the piano roll: one row up or down. Twelve make an octave.
consonance: The smooth, settled quality of intervals whose waves fit together simply.
dissonance: The rough, restless quality of intervals whose waves never settle.
chord: Several notes sounding together, heard as one object with a mood.
triad: The basic three-note chord: a root, a third, and a fifth, stacked.
root: The note a chord is built from and named after.
scale: A chosen set of notes defined by a pattern of steps, repeating every octave.
key: The gravity field of a scale: one note is home, and every other note is heard by its distance from home.
melody: A sequence of single notes heard as one continuous line with a shape.
contour: The overall shape of a melody: where it rises, peaks, and falls.
voice: One continuous musical line in a texture, whether or not anyone is singing.
circle of fifths: The twelve keys arranged in a wheel so neighbors differ by one note. Distance on the circle is harmonic distance.
diatonic: Belonging to the key: built only from the scale's own notes.
roman numeral: A chord named by its scale degree instead of its letter, so the name survives a key change.
pentatonic: A five-note scale with no semitones, so nothing in it clashes or demands resolution.
drone: A note held or repeated under everything else, giving the ear a fixed home to measure against.
equal temperament: Tuning that splits the octave into twelve identical steps, so every key is equally playable and equally, slightly, out of tune.
just intonation: Tuning built from pure small-number ratios: flawless in one key, unusable in the others.
cent: One hundredth of a semitone, the unit for measuring tiny differences in tuning.
